sources.name: Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern: Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills (S&P 500 incl. dividends)
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: All Items in U.S. City Average (CPIAUCNS), retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.notice: This product uses the FRED® API but is not endorsed or certified by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

method: Annual S&P 500 total returns (dividends reinvested) from Damodaran's dataset, calendar years 1928-2025.
Inflation: CPI-U, not seasonally adjusted, December-to-December change. Real return = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1.
Simple average = arithmetic mean of yearly returns. CAGR = the constant yearly return with the same ending value.
Contributions of $500 at the end of every month for 30 years. Each year's return is spread evenly over its 12 months; the 12% scenario uses the same rule, so it is exactly 12% a year.
Today's-dollars scenario: contributions keep constant purchasing power and returns are after inflation.
Rolling windows: every span of consecutive calendar years of the plan's length. Worst, median and best are ranked by the ending balance in today's dollars; the median is the middle window.
Actual annual return = the constant yearly return that turns the same contributions into the same ending balance (money-weighted).
Fund fees deducted: 0% a year. Taxes: none.
Example plan: $625 a month for 40 years; its projections compound the quoted rates as 1/12 of the annual rate each month. History is tested the same way as the main plan.
Cross-check: our 1928-2025 simple and compound averages match the ones the source reports.
caveats: US stocks were among the best-performing markets of the 20th century; other countries did worse (survivorship bias).
No taxes or trading costs, and the investor never stops, sells or changes the plan.
The S&P 500 itself dates from 1957; earlier years use its predecessor index, as compiled in the source.
Windows overlap: consecutive windows share all but one year, so they are not independent experiments.
Monthly CPI averages approximate year-end inflation.
History, not a forecast: past returns don't predict future returns.
